newsitem.title: USA: Texaco officers sued by shareholders over tapes.
newsitem.headline: Texaco officers sued by shareholders over tapes.

text.p: Texaco Inc.'s troubles mounted Thursday as it faced yet another lawsuit and the NAACP threatened to call on stockholders to dump the oil company's shares unless it improves opportunities for minorities.
Two Texaco shareholders sued Texaco officers, claiming corporate mismanagement fostered the alleged racist climate at the company that has tarnished its image in the last week.

"We are preparing to initiate a major divestiture campaign aimed at Texaco stock if we are unable to resolve this matter soon," said National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People President Kweisi Mfume.

"If a swift agreement is not reached and Texaco is unwilling to address the root causes of the problems there, we will work with our broad-based coalition to target Texaco's stock," Mfume said in a statement.
Texaco came under fire last week following allegations that its officials had planned to destroy evidence in a racial bias lawsuit filed by Texaco employees in 1994.
The allegations, which led to a federal probe, triggered calls this week by civil rights leaders for a boycott against Texaco products until the oil company settled the discrimination suit.
The employees are seeking payments of $71 million.
Civil rights leader Jesse Jackson this week called for a boycott of Texaco and said picketing of Texaco service stations would start Saturday.

The NAACP said Texaco's plan to improve the racial climate at the company should include specific goals and timetables for hiring and promoting minorities, contracting for goods and services from black-owned businesses and investing Texaco capital in black venture capital funds.
The NAACP said that it was "also considering informational picketing, targeted demonstrations and a coordinated boycott of Texaco products."
The lawsuit, filed in federal district court in Manhattan by shareholders Edith Citron and Martin Philip, is what is known as a shareholder derivative action on behalf and for the benefit of Texaco.

The suit names the current directors of Texaco; Texaco Chairman Peter Bijur; Robert Ulrich, former treasurer; and Richard Lundwall, former senior coordinator of personnel services in Texaco's finance department.

It claims the defendants breached their fiduciary duty by their "reckless or grossly negligent failure of the members of the board to adequately inform themselves as to the company's affairs and institute adequate systems of internal control and supervision."

The suit seeks unspecified damages from the 18 defendants. It seeks to force them to pay Texaco back all their salaries for the relevant period and to pay the damages Texaco may have to pay in the discrimination cases.

The suit is the latest faced by the company after transcripts of a tape recorded in 1994 were made public. In the transcripts, Texaco executives referred to minority workers as "niggers" and "black jelly beans."
Texaco has since claimed the words on the tape may be more benign.
A federal prosecutor in New York on Wednesday issued a subpoena to Texaco seeking documents related to racial discrimination allegations by six black employees.
Texaco's stock rose 37.5 cents to $98.375 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading.
